newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy to France seriously ill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy to France seriously ill.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador to France Pamela Harriman fell seriously ill in Paris on Monday and apparently suffered a stroke, U.S. officials said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Harriman's son Winston Spencer Churchill was at her bedside at the American hospital in the Paris suburb of Neuilly and "she's ill."
Another senior offical, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said, "I understand she's very, very ill. I heard it was a stroke."
Burns said Harriman, 76, had "fainted and fell ill."
CNN quoted a senior administration official as saying Harriman reportedly collapsed at home while exercising on Monday and was rushed to a hospital, where she remained unconscious.
The administration official said Harriman was "very close to death."

Harriman, whose full name is Pamela Digby Churchill Hayward Harriman, was born in Farnborough, England, and became a naturalised U.S. citizen after marrying her third husband, the late multimillionaire financier and diplomat W. Averell Harriman in 1971.

Her first marriage was during the Second World War at age 19 to Randolph Churchill, a journalist, hard-drinking rake and son of British leader Winston Churchill, who adored her and whom she fondly called "papa." They were divorced as the war ended but the marriage produced her only child, Winston Spencer Churchill.

Harriman was national co-chairman of the 1992 Clinton-Gore presidential campaign. After President Bill Clinton was elected in 1992, one of his first stops in Washington was a dinner party at Harriman's posh Georgetown home. For her favours to his party, Clinton named her ambassador to France in 1993, one of the plushest of diplomatic appointments.
